info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 2.1: Codicological Description and Hand-Authoring the TEI Header.

name.text: 01 Question: From Discursive Catalogues to Formal Metadata Systems

questiontext.text: Why are traditional discursive print catalogues inadequate for computational text analysis and cross-institutional discovery?

generalfeedback.text: Discursive print catalogues isolate codicological knowledge in human-readable silos; digital philology requires formal, machine-actionable schemas to enable computational analysis and cross-institutional discovery.

answer.text: They present metadata as unstructured narrative exposition and idiosyncratic prose that cannot be queried by relational databases or programmatic pipelines.

feedback.text: Correct. Discursive essays lock codicological knowledge in human-readable silos that lack machine-actionable data structures.

answer.text: They fail to record essential paleographical observations such as script classification or ink colour.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Traditional catalogues often provide rich, erudite paleographical descriptions, but do so in unstructured prose.

answer.text: They were published exclusively in vernacular languages rather than standardized scholarly Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many early catalogues were written in Latin, yet their flowing narrative structure remains unqueryable computationally.

answer.text: They intentionally omit institutional shelfmarks to prevent unauthorised reproduction of rare manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Traditional catalogues recorded shelfmarks, but institutional variation in syntax and abbreviations hinders automated aggregation.

name.text: 02 Question: The Epistemology of Manuscript Modeling: FRBRoo and LRMoo

questiontext.text: In the FRBRoo ontological model, why is a premodern handwritten codex classified as an F4 Manifestation Singleton rather than an F3 Manifestation Product Type?

generalfeedback.text: Modern print catalogues model mass-produced publication types, but premodern manuscripts are manifestation singletons whose unique physical embodiment cannot be separated from their textual witness.

answer.text: Every handwritten manuscript is a unique historical artifact whose physical embodiment cannot be separated from its textual realization.

feedback.text: Correct. Unlike mass-produced print editions where thousands of items share one manifestation type, a manuscript singleton is a singular, unrepeatable historical event.

answer.text: A manuscript contains multiple distinct intellectual works bound together in a single volume.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Composite contents occur in both print and manuscripts; singleton status derives from unique physical production rather than multi-text anthologizing.

answer.text: Handwritten codices are preserved exclusively in single institutional repositories rather than circulating publicly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical location or circulation restrictions do not define the bibliographic ontology of manifestation singletons.

answer.text: The manuscript's scribe is considered both the intellectual author and the physical printer of the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The scribe is an agent of transmission; the singleton classification addresses the identity of the physical manifestation itself.

name.text: 03 Question: Why We Hand-Write XML Markup Before Running a Validator

questiontext.text: What is the primary pedagogical and methodological purpose of hand-authoring a TEI Header before using schema-aware editors or AI tools?

generalfeedback.text: Writing XML markup by hand forces conscious decision-making for every codicological feature, establishing the authoritative human ground truth required to evaluate automated tools.

answer.text: It forces the editor to make every architectural and codicological decision explicitly, establishing an authoritative human ground truth.

feedback.text: Correct. Manual markup slows down analytical gaze and avoids premature reliance on IDE defaults or probabilistic AI predictions.

answer.text: Hand-written XML documents are automatically exempt from formal RELAX NG schema validation rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand-written markup must still undergo rigorous schema validation; manual drafting establishes the baseline to test against.

answer.text: Manual entry is the only method that guarantees 100% syntactic well-formedness on the initial draft.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hand-authoring is prone to typographical defects, which makes subsequent automated validation essential.

answer.text: Modern XML parsers reject files that contain metadata generated by automated autocomplete algorithms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parsers evaluate syntax and schema grammar without regard to whether text was typed manually or generated by software.

name.text: 04 Question: XML Fundamentals: The Syntax of Tree Structures

questiontext.text: Which condition must be met for an XML document to be considered syntactically well-formed?

generalfeedback.text: XML enforces strict syntactic well-formedness—single root, perfect nesting, exact case matching, and quoted attributes—with zero tolerance for parsing defects.

answer.text: It must adhere strictly to basic grammar rules: a single root element, matching case-sensitive closing tags, clean nesting, and quoted attribute values.

feedback.text: Correct. Well-formedness is the baseline syntactic requirement of XML; any violation causes an immediate fatal parser crash.

answer.text: It must be successfully validated against an external DTD, RELAX NG, or W3C XML Schema definition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conformance to an external schema defines validity, which is a higher-level requirement than syntactic well-formedness.

answer.text: All text nodes must contain fewer than 500 characters to prevent memory buffer overflows.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML places no arbitrary length restrictions on element text content.

answer.text: Every element must possess a unique xml:id attribute declared in the document header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. While xml:id is common in TEI for cross-referencing, it is not a syntactic requirement for general XML well-formedness.

name.text: 05 Question: Elements, Attributes, and the Hierarchy of Containment

questiontext.text: In TEI XML document design, what distinguishes the appropriate usage of elements from that of attributes?

generalfeedback.text: Elements define hierarchical containers and primary content, while attributes supply qualifying metadata, categorical types, machine-readable values, and external links.

answer.text: Elements represent structural containers and primary narrative content, whereas attributes provide qualifying metadata, datatypes, and machine-readable values.

feedback.text: Correct. Elements can nest child elements and form hierarchies; attributes hold flat, unparsed qualifying data inside opening tags.

answer.text: Elements hold only plain numerical data, while attributes contain long discursive prose descriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reverse is true: discursive prose belongs in element text, while attributes supply concise metadata or normalized values.

answer.text: Attributes can contain nested child elements, whereas elements are restricted to flat string literals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Attributes cannot contain child tags; only elements can establish hierarchical parent-child containment.

answer.text: Elements are ignored by schema validators, while attributes are the only components subject to datatype constraints.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validators enforce strict content models and datatypes on both elements and their attributes.

name.text: 06 Question: The Anatomy of the TEI Document Envelope

questiontext.text: What is the structural relationship between <teiHeader> and <text> within a standard TEI document?

generalfeedback.text: A TEI document cleanly separates descriptive metadata in the `` from transcribed primary text in ``, ensuring the digital edition remains fully documented and auditable.

answer.text: They are mandatory sibling elements enclosed directly within the root <TEI> envelope, cleanly separating descriptive metadata from transcribed primary text.

feedback.text: Correct. The TEI architecture strictly isolates administrative and codicological metadata in the header from the transcribed source in the text carrier.

answer.text: The <teiHeader> is nested inside the <front> division of the <text> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The header is a top-level sibling of <text>, not a child of front matter.

answer.text: The <text> element is optional, while the <teiHeader> must enclose all diplomatic transcription lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic transcriptions belong in <text> (or <facsimile>), not inside the metadata header.

answer.text: The <teiHeader> is compiled into a standalone binary file that replaces the root <TEI> element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both branches remain plain text XML nodes under the single root <TEI>.

name.text: 07 Question: The Digital Edition as Artifact: fileDesc and titleStmt

questiontext.text: When encoding the <titleStmt> inside <fileDesc>, what does the <title> element record?

generalfeedback.text: The `` and `` document the digital edition as an independent intellectual publication, distinguishing the digital editors from the ancient scribes.

answer.text: The title of the digital scholarly edition and project, rather than the ancient title of the physical manuscript.

feedback.text: Correct. The <fileDesc> documents the digital file as an independent intellectual publication created by modern editors.

answer.text: The incipit and initial rubric of the primary biblical or literary work in the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ancient rubrics and incipits are recorded in <msContents>, not in the digital edition's title statement.

answer.text: The modern institutional shelfmark assigned by the holding repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Shelfmarks are catalogued in <msIdentifier> via <idno>.

answer.text: The commercial publication title of the printed facsimile edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <titleStmt> identifies the current electronic text edition being authored.

name.text: 08 Question: Encoding Intellectual Responsibility and Contributions

questiontext.text: How does the TEI <respStmt> element establish scholarly accountability within a collaborative digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: Granular intellectual credit and editorial accountability are established using ``, linking specific scholarly tasks to identified contributors via `@xml:id`.

answer.text: It explicitly pairs a specific scholarly responsibility (<resp>) with an identified contributor (<name>) possessing a unique @xml:id.

feedback.text: Correct. This allows later revision logs, apparatus entries, and transcription layers to attribute decisions directly to specific project collaborators.

answer.text: It assigns legal copyright ownership to institutional funding agencies while anonymizing student encoders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <respStmt> provides transparent attribution for individual contributors rather than obscuring names.

answer.text: It automatically verifies whether an encoder's transcription matches the underlying high-resolution image pixels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <respStmt> records human editorial roles, not programmatic image verification.

answer.text: It encrypts editorial change logs to prevent unauthorized modification by secondary researchers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI metadata is designed for open-access transparency, not cryptographic access control.

name.text: 09 Question: Digital Distribution and Licensing: publicationStmt

questiontext.text: Which requirement is essential when declaring publication dates and distribution conditions in <publicationStmt>?

generalfeedback.text: The `` establishes the legal and institutional availability of the digital edition, recording open-access licenses, distributors, and ISO-standard dates.

answer.text: Dates should include machine-readable ISO 8601 values in @when attributes, accompanied by formal licensing declarations.

feedback.text: Correct. Enforcing ISO date standards (such as YYYY-MM-DD) allows automated harvesters and bibliographic indexers to process temporal metadata deterministically.

answer.text: The publication statement must contain the full unredacted legal contract between the university and commercial publishers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard digital editions declare open-access licenses (such as Creative Commons) via <licence> rather than commercial contracts.

answer.text: All manuscripts must be placed under public domain dedications without attribution requirements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Projects frequently use CC BY licenses requiring attribution; the schema permits various licensing terms.

answer.text: The distributor element must point to a physical printing press located in the country of origin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <publicationStmt> records the digital distributor and electronic publication venue.

name.text: 10 Question: The Source of Record: sourceDesc as the Codicological Anchor

questiontext.text: Why is the <msDesc> element placed inside <sourceDesc> in a manuscript-based digital edition?

generalfeedback.text: In manuscript-based editions, `` houses the `` module, anchoring the digital transcription to a specific historical codex.

answer.text: It anchors the digital transcription directly to the physical codex, providing a comprehensive, nested description of the historical witness.

feedback.text: Correct. In manuscript editions, <sourceDesc> houses <msDesc> to declare that the digital text is derived from that specific physical artifact.

answer.text: It indicates that the manuscript description was automatically scraped from an online Wikipedia article.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <sourceDesc> contains authoritative archival metadata authored by project editors.

answer.text: It separates modern printed secondary sources from ancient Greek inscriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <sourceDesc> can hold various sources, but <msDesc> specifically models handwritten codices.

answer.text: It converts the TEI XML document into a standalone IIIF presentation manifest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI and IIIF are distinct standards; <msDesc> models codicological data within the XML tree.

name.text: 11 Question: Anchoring the Physical Object: The msIdentifier Architecture

questiontext.text: What is the hierarchical function of the <msIdentifier> element in a manuscript description?

generalfeedback.text: The `` provides the definitive archival address of the physical object, combining country, settlement, repository, shelfmark, and standard scholarly sigla.

answer.text: To provide an unambiguous archival address combining country, settlement, repository, collection, and unique shelfmark.

feedback.text: Correct. <msIdentifier> gives the exact geographic and institutional coordinates required to locate the physical artifact.

answer.text: To list all modern critical editions and translations published of the manuscript's texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern editions and bibliography belong in <additional> or <listBibl>.

answer.text: To record the names of the ancient scribes and modern digital encoders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scribes are catalogued in <handDesc> and encoders in <titleStmt>.

answer.text: To calculate the geometric aspect ratio of the parchment folios automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical dimensions are recorded in <physDesc> under <dimensions>.

name.text: 12 Question: Case Study: Locating and Identifying Codex Marchalianus (Vat. gr. 2125)

questiontext.text: Why is Codex Marchalianus (Vat. gr. 2125, Rahlfs Q) considered a uniquely demanding exemplar for TEI codicological description?

generalfeedback.text: Codex Marchalianus (Vat. gr. 2125) exemplifies a multi-layered sixth-century prophetic witness whose complex physical and marginal features demand rigorous TEI codicological description.

answer.text: It combines a 6th-century uncial primary prophetic text with thousands of contemporary and later marginal hexaplaric variants and patristic scholia.

feedback.text: Correct. The complex physical stratification of primary text and dense marginalia requires precise paleographical, layout, and decorative encoding.

answer.text: It is the only surviving manuscript in the world written entirely in golden ink on purple-dyed vellum.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Marchalianus is written in brown iron-gall ink on standard parchment, not purple chrysography.

answer.text: It was completely destroyed in 1968, making photographic facsimiles the only surviving physical evidence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The codex is safely preserved in the Vatican Library vault; Ceriani published its facsimile in 1890.

answer.text: It contains no quire signatures or foliation marks, preventing physical collation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It contains intact Greek quire signatures (αʹ to νβʹ) across its 52 regular quaterniones.

name.text: 13 Question: Mapping the Intellectual Contents: msContents and msItem

questiontext.text: How does <msContents> structure the multiple texts contained within an anthological or biblical codex?

generalfeedback.text: The `` element structures the intellectual works in a codex into discrete `` nodes, mapping each work to its physical folio range via ``.

answer.text: It encapsulates each distinct intellectual work in a sequential <msItem> node, linking it to physical folios via <locus>.

feedback.text: Correct. <msContents> models the intellectual contents as an ordered list of <msItem> elements mapped to leaf ranges.

answer.text: It merges all texts into a single unbroken paragraph to conserve file storage size.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI structures each work independently to enable granular searching and indexing.

answer.text: It arranges works alphabetically by Latin title regardless of their physical sequence in the volume.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <msItem> elements follow the actual physical sequence of texts in the manuscript.

answer.text: It automatically translates ancient Greek texts into modern English prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <msContents> catalogues metadata about the works rather than generating automatic translations.

name.text: 14 Question: Titles, Attributions, and Textual Boundaries

questiontext.text: Why are elements like <rubric>, <incipit>, and <explicit> essential when cataloguing historical manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: Dedicated elements like ``, ``, and `` record the exact scribal framing formulas that mark textual boundaries in the codex.

answer.text: Manuscripts lack modern title pages, relying instead on distinctive scribal opening formulas, initial text lines, and closing blessings to delimit works.

feedback.text: Correct. Recording exact scribal framing formulas preserves diplomatic fidelity and enables text identification when titles are missing or damaged.

answer.text: They allow automated search engines to bypass the need for standardized authority titles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standardized titles in <title> are still used alongside historical framing formulas.

answer.text: They are mandatory XML tags required to enable image zooming in web browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Image zooming is handled by IIIF protocols, not TEI textual boundary elements.

answer.text: They automatically correct orthographical spelling variations introduced by medieval scribes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These elements record the diplomatic readings as they appear in the manuscript.

name.text: 15 Question: The Physical Description Envelope: physDesc and Materiality

questiontext.text: What is the core function of the <physDesc> module within a TEI manuscript description?

generalfeedback.text: The `` module formalizes the material properties of the manuscript into dedicated sub-elements for support, layout, script, decoration, and binding.

answer.text: To formalize the physical materiality of the artifact into dedicated sub-elements for support, layout, script, decoration, and binding.

feedback.text: Correct. <physDesc> provides structured containers (such as <objectDesc>, <handDesc>, and <decoDesc>) to model physical book craft.

answer.text: To store high-resolution JPEG image files directly within the XML document tree.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binary images are stored externally and referenced via URIs or IIIF manifests.

answer.text: To record the modern financial valuation and insurance appraisal of the codex.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <physDesc> focuses on codicological and paleographical features, not commercial appraisal.

answer.text: To translate medieval Greek theological treatises into standardized modern XML markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Intellectual translation belongs in <text>; <physDesc> models physical attributes.

name.text: 16 Question: Support and Dimensions: objectDesc and supportDesc

questiontext.text: Why does TEI encode manuscript measurements using both @quantity attributes and human-readable text in <dimensions>?

generalfeedback.text: The `` captures the physical medium and leaf dimensions, using `@quantity` and `@unit` attributes to provide machine-actionable measurements.

answer.text: Attributes supply normalized numbers and units for computational calculations, while element text preserves descriptive nuances.

feedback.text: Correct. Dual encoding allows algorithms to compute aspect ratios and execute dimension queries without parsing raw strings.

answer.text: XML syntax requires all numerical values to be entered twice to prevent data corruption during network transmission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML does not require duplicate entry for error checking; the practice serves dual computational and human reading needs.

answer.text: The attribute stores the dimensions in inches while the element text is restricted to millimetres.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard digital codicology uses metric units (typically mm) specified in the @unit attribute.

answer.text: Attributes are visible to human website visitors while element text is hidden from search engines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Element text is readily indexed by search engines and displayed in browsers.

name.text: 17 Question: Foliation, Pagination, and Extent

questiontext.text: Why is documenting the history and placement of leaf numbers in <foliation> critical for textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: The `` element documents the history and location of leaf-numbering systems, resolving discrepancies between historical and modern citations.

answer.text: Manuscripts often contain multiple conflicting numbering schemes from different centuries, which must be disambiguated for citation integrity.

feedback.text: Correct. Resolving discrepancies between medieval ink numbers and modern pencil foliation ensures that citations to specific folios remain verifiable.

answer.text: Foliation tags are required by law before a manuscript can be exported across national borders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Foliation is an archival and scholarly descriptive practice, not an export customs regulation.

answer.text: A manuscript cannot be bound into a physical volume unless its leaves are numbered sequentially in Arabic numerals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many medieval manuscripts were unnumbered or used quire signatures rather than leaf foliation.

answer.text: Automated OCR tools will refuse to transcribe any image that lacks an explicit <foliation> tag in its header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. OCR and HTR engines process image pixels directly regardless of TEI header tags.

name.text: 18 Question: Codicological Collation Formulas: collation

questiontext.text: In codicological description, what does the collation formula 1-52^8 signify?

generalfeedback.text: The `` element formalizes the physical structure of quires, leaf counts, and quire signatures, exposing the mechanical construction of the codex.

answer.text: The manuscript consists of 52 regular quires of 8 leaves (quaterniones) each, totaling 416 folios.

feedback.text: Correct. Ker's standard algebraic notation indicates quire numbers followed by a superscript indicating leaf count per gathering.

answer.text: The text was copied by 52 distinct scribes working over an 8-year period.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation formulas describe the physical gathering of leaves, not scribal labor timelines.

answer.text: The manuscript contains 1 to 52 chapters divided across 8 thematic volumes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The formula represents physical gatherings of bifolia, not textual chapter divisions.

answer.text: Leaves 1 through 52 were damaged on the 8th line of each page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation formulas model quire architecture rather than physical page damage.

name.text: 19 Question: Layout Description and Page Architecture: layoutDesc

questiontext.text: How does the <layoutDesc> element support downstream transcription and automated handwriting recognition?

generalfeedback.text: The `` and `` elements capture the mise-en-page, specifying column counts, written lines, ruling techniques, and margin widths.

answer.text: It formally specifies column counts, written line counts, ruling techniques, and margin dimensions used to calibrate baseline models.

feedback.text: Correct. Layout parameters define the page geometry required by HTR tools (like Transkribus) to segment columns and detect text baselines.

answer.text: It automatically re-formats the physical parchment leaves to fit modern widescreen computer monitors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <layoutDesc> records historical page dimensions, not modern display screen scaling.

answer.text: It dictates the CSS styling rules used to render HTML web editions in modern browsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI describes semantic and codicological data; web presentation is controlled by stylesheets.

answer.text: It translates abbreviations and ligatures into expanded Unicode Greek characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual normalization occurs in transcription markup, not in layout descriptions.

name.text: 20 Question: Paleographic Analysis: The handDesc and handNote Elements

questiontext.text: Why must each <handNote> declared in <handDesc> possess a unique @xml:id?

generalfeedback.text: The `` and `` elements document distinct scribal hands, establishing unique `@xml:id` handles for granular paleographic attribution in transcriptions.

answer.text: To establish persistent identifier handles that can be referenced by @hand attributes on specific words, lines, or marginal additions in the transcription.

feedback.text: Correct. Assigning @xml:id="h1" allows transcription tags like <add hand="#h1"> to link text directly to that scribal hand.

answer.text: To register the scribe's legal identity with modern national copyright databases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ancient scribes have no modern copyright registrations; IDs serve internal document linking.

answer.text: To satisfy XML well-formedness rules that require all elements to have unique identifiers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. xml:id is an optional attribute in XML syntax, though required by project Schematron rules for hand linking.

answer.text: To prevent other scholars from editing the paleographical description of that hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Identifiers enable machine navigation and attribution, not write-protection.

name.text: 21 Question: Decorations, Miniatures, and Marginal Signs: decoDesc

questiontext.text: In biblical manuscripts like Codex Marchalianus, why are critical signs like asterisks and obels catalogued in <decoDesc>?

generalfeedback.text: The `` module catalogues artistic illuminations, decorated initials, and critical philological signs like asterisks and obels.

answer.text: They represent specialized graphic and philological signs marking additions and omissions relative to the Hexaplaric Hebrew and Greek texts.

feedback.text: Correct. Origenian signs are vital philological data that straddle the boundary between decorative symbols and text-critical apparatus.

answer.text: They are decorative errors created when the scribe's pen accidentally dripped ink onto the parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Asterisks (※) and obels (÷) are deliberate, structured text-critical symbols.

answer.text: They indicate that the manuscript was condemned as heretical by ecclesiastical censors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hexaplaric signs indicate textual alignment with the Hebrew text in Origen's Hexapla.

answer.text: They are modern watermarks pressed into the paper during nineteenth-century rebinding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These signs were written in the 6th and 7th centuries in the manuscript margins.

name.text: 22 Question: The Binding and Structural Protection: bindingDesc

questiontext.text: Why is the attribute @contemporary="false" critical when encoding a manuscript's <bindingDesc>?

generalfeedback.text: The `` documents the bookbinding materials, sewing structure, and conservation history, explicitly distinguishing contemporary bindings from modern rebinding.

answer.text: It explicitly indicates that the binding was produced in a later period than the leaves, preventing scholars from mistaking modern rebinding for original late antique craft.

feedback.text: Correct. Most surviving ancient codices were rebound in the early modern or modern era; documenting non-contemporary bindings preserves historical accuracy.

answer.text: It declares that the binding is damaged and cannot be safely handled in a library reading room.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical condition is recorded in <condition>; contemporary status addresses historical synchronicity.

answer.text: It instructs digital viewers to display the manuscript without rendering its binding covers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The attribute informs codicological metadata rather than suppressing image display.

answer.text: It certifies that the binding materials were sourced from synthetic modern polymers rather than animal hides.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A 1968 morocco leather binding is non-contemporary with a 6th-century codex despite using animal leather.

name.text: 23 Question: The Chronological Lifecycle: The history Element

questiontext.text: How does the TEI <history> module organize the temporal lifecycle of a manuscript artifact?

generalfeedback.text: The `` element traces the temporal lifecycle of the codex, dividing its history into origin, sequential provenance transfers, and modern institutional acquisition.

answer.text: By dividing history into discrete, sequential stages: production (<origin>), custodial transfers (<provenance>), and institutional accession (<acquisition>).

feedback.text: Correct. This event-centric structure aligns TEI metadata directly with Linked Open Data ontologies like CIDOC-CRM.

answer.text: By generating a continuous prose biography that merges scribal production with modern restoration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI structures historical lifecycle into distinct, typed event elements.

answer.text: By recording only the current twentieth-century archival acquisition while omitting premodern owners.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Premodern ownership transfers are comprehensively modeled in sequential <provenance> nodes.

answer.text: By converting historical Julian dates into radioactive carbon-dating decay curves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <history> records documentary and paleographical lifecycle events.

name.text: 24 Question: Dating and Localizing the Manuscript: origin

questiontext.text: When dating a manuscript without an explicit colophon, how does TEI represent palaeographical date ranges and uncertainty in <origDate>?

generalfeedback.text: The `` element uses ISO 8601 attributes like `@notBefore` and `@notAfter` to represent historical dating ranges and palaeographical uncertainty.

answer.text: By using ISO 8601 interval attributes (@notBefore and @notAfter) combined with qualitative certainty attributes (@cert and @evidence).

feedback.text: Correct. Attributes like notBefore="0550" notAfter="0599" cert="medium" provide machine-computable boundaries while recording scholarly uncertainty.

answer.text: By writing conversational approximate phrases like 'around the late sixth century' directly into the @when attribute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Machine-readable date attributes require strict ISO 8601 formatting; prose descriptions belong in element content.

answer.text: By assigning an arbitrary single year and omitting any indication of editorial uncertainty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Forcing an exact year misrepresents historical knowledge and distorts temporal filtering.

answer.text: By leaving the date field completely blank whenever a colophon is absent.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Palaeographical date estimates are valuable scholarship and should be encoded with explicit bounding attributes.

name.text: 25 Question: Custodial Chain and Migration: The provenance Sequence

questiontext.text: Why is the custodial history of a codex encoded as a sequence of discrete <provenance> elements rather than a single narrative block?

generalfeedback.text: The custodial chain is modeled as a chronological sequence of `` elements, enabling computational tracking of manuscript migrations across time and geography.

answer.text: Each distinct transfer of ownership can be assigned independent dates, places, and agents, enabling knowledge graphs to track migrations across time and space.

feedback.text: Correct. Discrete provenance events can be transformed into RDF triples and mapped spatially in projects like Mapping Manuscript Migrations.

answer.text: XML schemas prohibit <provenance> elements from containing more than one sentence of text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Elements can contain paragraphs, but discrete events allow granular temporal and spatial modeling.

answer.text: Multiple provenance tags are required to prove legal title in international cultural property restitution claims.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance markup serves scholarly and archival discovery rather than legal litigation.

answer.text: A new provenance tag must be generated each time a patron checks out the manuscript in a reading room.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern reading room consultations are administrative records, not custodial provenance transfers.

name.text: 26 Question: Administrative and Acquisition Metadata: acquisition and additional

questiontext.text: What is the distinct role of the <additional> container following the <history> element in <msDesc>?

generalfeedback.text: The `` and `` elements document the institutional accession history, cataloguing sources, and related secondary bibliography for the manuscript.

answer.text: It holds supplementary administrative records, secondary bibliography (<listBibl>), and references to digital surrogates and microfilms.

feedback.text: Correct. <additional> catalogues external documentation, catalogues, and secondary scholarly literature about the codex.

answer.text: It stores the full transcribed text of any missing folios discovered after publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcribed texts belong in <text>, not in header administrative containers.

answer.text: It contains the compiled binary machine code for the online edition's web server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI is a document encoding standard, not a software executable container.

answer.text: It serves as a temporary quarantine area for unvalidated XML tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All elements in the document must be valid according to the active schema.

name.text: 27 Question: Common Syntax Traps in Hand-Authoring TEI Headers

questiontext.text: Which coding mistake in an XML text node will cause an immediate fatal parser crash during well-formedness checking?

generalfeedback.text: Hand-written XML requires rigorous manual checking for unescaped characters, case mismatches, missing quotes, and improper tag containment.

answer.text: Writing a bare ampersand (&) in text content instead of the escaped entity reference &.

feedback.text: Correct. Bare ampersands conflict with XML entity delimiter syntax and cause fatal parser termination.

answer.text: Using British spelling conventions (such as 'colour') instead of American English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Natural language orthography has no effect on XML well-formedness.

answer.text: Indenting child elements with two spaces instead of four spaces.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Whitespace between tags is not syntactically invalid in XML.

answer.text: Writing comments using standard <!-- comment --> syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Comment syntax is fully valid and supported in well-formed XML.

name.text: 28 Question: Building the Ground Truth: The Student's Primary Witness Header

questiontext.text: What deliverable constitutes the foundational human ground truth authored in Lesson 2.1?

generalfeedback.text: Hand-authoring your selected manuscript's complete `` creates the foundational XML ground truth for the remainder of the semester.

name.text: 29 Question: Preparing for Wednesday's Audit: Deliverables and Configuration

questiontext.text: Why must the hand-authored XML file be committed to Git version control at the conclusion of Lesson 2.1 without further editing?

generalfeedback.text: Committing your hand-written XML file to Git freezes your manual ground truth, establishing the baseline for tomorrow's deterministic schema audit.

answer.text: To freeze the unassisted manual baseline so that tomorrow's deterministic schema audit measures genuine human intuition against formal rules.

feedback.text: Correct. Committing to Git preserves the untouched manual ground truth needed for quantitative error scoring in subsequent labs.

answer.text: Because Git repositories automatically repair any syntax errors in XML files overnight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git is a version control system that stores exact snapshots; it does not modify file contents.

answer.text: Because university policy requires all student assignments to be publicly pushed to remote servers immediately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The local commit preserves the audit trail; pushing is governed by project session protocols.

answer.text: To convert the XML file into an immutable PDF companion document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDF compilation is a distinct downstream build step, not a property of Git commits.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Header as an Argument in Structural Form

questiontext.text: Why is a TEI Header properly understood as an intellectual argument rather than mere administrative metadata?

generalfeedback.text: A TEI Header is an explicit scholarly argument that translates physical manuscript materiality into a formal, auditable digital data architecture.

answer.text: Every decision regarding quire structure, hand attribution, date boundaries, and content segmentation represents an explicit, testable philological interpretation.

feedback.text: Correct. Encoding codicological metadata translates physical materiality into a formal, structured thesis about the artifact's production and history.

answer.text: It contains rhetorical polemics defending the editor's religious beliefs against secular critics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument is codicological and methodological, not confessional or polemical.

answer.text: It is designed to replace the need for scholars to ever consult physical manuscripts again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital descriptions enhance and guide consultation of physical witnesses rather than claiming to replace them.

answer.text: It is authored by artificial intelligence algorithms that operate independently of human scholarship.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The header represents human editorial scholarship structured within a computational schema.
